Gnaws at the nerves and bludgeons the senses until submission-to humanity's helplessness in the face of the ancient world's elemental power-is the only recourse.
Even though some sections feel rushed and it falls apart at the end, every part of it is memorable.
Does "In the Earth" run off the rails into addled sensationalism in the end? Yes. But while it's steaming ahead at full power, Wheatley's magic mushroom trip is a grueling yet exhilarating ride.
In The Earth feeds the indiscriminate appetites of gorehounds and bong-rippers alike. Everyone else may find it as ghastly boring as the violence is just plain ghastly.
Sinister and hilarious, psychedelic yet grounded, absurdist while still gripping, In the Earth will take root in you.
The film rattles apart as it goes along...
Wheatley crafts a plague film that isn't necessarily about a plague, but that captures the anxiety and fear of invisible forces beyond our control impelling us, unknowingly, into danger.
"Earth" deserves points for originality, but grows wobbly by its end.

title: Wrath of Man | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Fine form with some old-fashioned shoot-’em-up fun.
For all its flip-flops, there's never anything engaging or surprising. Very perfunctory.
A leaden, blood-spattered and painfully predictable trudge towards an anticlimax that is as joyless as it is expected.
Rough at the edges and with a propensity for cartoonish violence, this is an action caper hewn in the image of its star.

Guy Ritchie delivers a nice surprise: an LA neo-noir with high-voltage action and an ice-cube-cool Statham. If it gets a bit tangled up in its time-hopping reveals, it's largely an enjoyable, rattlesnake-mean thriller.
Nothing in Wrath of Man suggests that Ritchie is having fun anymore-not with the crime genre, and not with filmmaking.
There is menace, a dull darkness and stillness, as if he's watched "Heat" too many times.
Unsurprisingly, this stripped-down soundtrack serves as the perfect counterpoint for Ritchie's direction, adding an element of the funereal to even the most visceral action sequence.
It hits every one of those genres nice and hard, and it pops. It's going to go at number two among my [favorite] Guy Ritchie films.
It's just a dirty piece of fun, and I enjoyed it!
Taken on its terms, the movie isn't terrible strictly as mindless escapism. But beyond the most basic, visceral thrills, Wrath of Man's bitter fruit yields a slim harvest.

Wrath of Man: a Jason Statham movie directed by Guy Ritchie. Check. A revenge thriller wearing the clothes of a heist thriller: a savory treat-within-a-treat, like a bacon-wrapped sausage. Check, check.

Gritting his teeth, the antihero action star boldly goes where other over-50s like Liam Neeson have gone before, riding the vengeance train in a violent, stunt-filled action thriller that takes no prisoners.
Things get so convoluted if you told me the cast and crew were making up new plot elements as shooting went along I'd be tempted to believe it.
Wrath of Man is all body count, and its self-seriousness is exhausting. This isn't Ritchie's Heat; it's his The Tax Collector.
"Wrath of Man" is a Guy Ritchie film that even his detractors might like.
Ritchie is either off his game a tad, or his decision to play things down is a mistake. Nothing is as clever as it could be.
The writing in Wrath of Man isn't just bad. It's your-co-worker-signed-up-for-a-weekend-drama-workshop bad.
"Wrath" delivers what Statham and Ritchie's bloodthirstier fans are probably looking for, but it seems unlikely to win either of them new ones.
Wrath is just another loose bag of lizard-brain thrills and wood-block dialogue: too ugly to be camp, too grimly familiar to feel new.

title: The Mitchells vs. the Machines | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Putting the "fun" in "dysfunction" is what The Mitchells vs. The Machines is about, and what family doesn't have some issues?
It's the kind of movie you immediately want to watch again and again.

In its celebration of these characters... this film demonstrates how indispensable every single one of us is, and how much those living with disabilities have to offer the world, if only people took the time to notice.
In "The Mitchells vs. the Machines," family life is a brilliant, ever-changing collage.
The voice casting is terrific, and Coleman is especially funny...
A dazzling and wildly charming family adventure brimming with creativity and heart. The Mitchells vs. the Machines is bound to be one of the best animated features of 2021.
This is a perfect movie for the whole family, which is an all-too-rare thing to find.
Take away the serrated satirical edges, and you're still left with a surprisingly delightful story about a dysfunctional family learning how to connect again.
Whether through experience or intuition, Rianda and Rowe clearly understand animated comedy from the inside out; the gags stretch and snap as readily as the family tensions.
Casting Olivia Colman as the voice of a demonic AI is only the first stroke of genius in this sprightly animated movie, produced by Phil Lord and Chris Miller.
Sharp, funny, and self-aware.
If it doesn't quite have the emotional kick of a Pixar movie it is only because the creative investment has gone elsewhere. Mostly into the hyper-powered pacing.
The unwaveringly sweet, animated example "The Mitchells vs the Machines," largely avoids the genre's worst cliches for a tear-jerking adventure ripe with apocalyptic fun.
At times it can't seem to stick to a single story thread for more than a minute. But its emotional design and trajectory are crystal clear, and the chaos feels like part of a grand plan.
While the themes are flimsy, The Mitchells vs. the Machines has plenty that's worthwhile.
The film's overall aesthetic is a pleasing blend of naturalistic drawings, cartoonier designs and Heavy Metal magazine futurism.

Further proof that producers Phil Lord and Christopher Miller are an animation brand as reliable as Disney or Pixar, and a good deal more likely to provide something that's not only sturdy but genuinely surprising.
In brief, intriguing flashes, it manages to exude a sensibility that's darker, spikier, and more idiosyncratic than most other animated films you'd plop your kid in front of.
"The Mitchells vs. the Machines" not only has laughably eccentric characters but also a script packed with bonkers, fast-paced action - with elaborate, wild visuals to match.

The Mitchells vs the Machines is like an encounter with a sentient doodle pad, crammed with ideas that might be the cleverest things anyone's ever thought of, or the most ludicrous, or probably a jumble of both.

title: We Broke Up | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: We Broke Up is a breeze to watch thanks to its fully-committed leads, who go wherever the story takes them.
There are a million reasons why couples break up. If only We Broke Up had landed on one, they might have really had something here.

A relationship isn't necessarily a waste of time just because it doesn't lead to the altar, Rosenberg affectingly reminds us, just as a movie isn't necessarily a waste of time just because it doesn't seem to be leading anywhere else.
Harper and Cash are ideal, and the writing and direction make this one broken affair to remember.
The best thing about it is William Jackson Harper... If you're looking for something that doesn't just follow the tropes of a romantic comedy, this might just be the film for you.
This was okay -- maybe even more than that... It's just never as funny as its first joke.

While "We Broke Up" is focused, lean and heartfelt, it does feel at times a bit insubstantial. It's missing the "why" at the center of this conflict, particularly with Lori, who remains an opaque character.
Cash and Harper have an oddly appealing chemistry. Their intimate portrayals make Lori and Doug feel sincere.
Although the relationship at the heart of We Broke Up may be messy and complicated, Rosenberg ties all of the story's elements together into a neat, bittersweet package.
The film's ambitions are impressive, but the characters are too thinly written to support them, despite the best efforts of the actors.
Rosenberg can't stick the landing after so much mediocre clowning.
"We Broke Up" catches a rom-com ripple and rides it toward sweet laughs and some authentic insights.
The film is tense through scenes that might have been funny and maudlin when addressing the emotional stakes for the former couple. The overwhelming impression is that of shrillness.

title: Together Together | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Together Together suffers a little from being too polite, as a comedy it lacks snarl, and as a drama it lacks, well, event.
Just Helms' and Harrison's expressions at these situations are enough to bring about chuckles.
Harrison is tremendous.

Beckwith's script does have a few moments of grace and humor. Helms gets a particularly beautiful monologue about why he wants a child... But there are far more clichés, contrivances and threads left unnecessarily dangling.

Watching Matt and Anna discover the parameters of their friendship, and the impact they have on each other's lives, is quite rewarding. Both Helms and Harrison nail the fluid nature of the tonal shifts as their bond tightens, loosens, and tightens.
Opposite Ed Helms, the likable Patti Harrison is funny and endearing as a surrogate mom in a comedy that's a joy to experience.
"Together Together" is a sweet film about connection that leaves some large questions unanswered and open-ended.
Together Together is not just smart, it's sneaky-smart.

Beckwith's film never condemns going it alone. Rather, it finds the hopefulness in what society might deem hopeless, reminding us to go after what we want, while savoring togetherness, in any form it takes, along the way.
Sweet, funny, a little melancholy and a little obvious, Together Together is an odd-couple parable with a fertile comedic premise.
The easeful, unvarnished rapport Helms and Harrison generate through their touching performances is the steady cradle to this brisk two-hander.
That the softness of the whole endeavor never quite turns to squish is a lot to do with how naturally the principals underplay it and how genuine their G-rated chemistry seems.
"Together Together" is a big warm hug of a movie, a pregnancy dramedy that upends expectations and pulls on your heart strings with a tale of two very different best friends.

Harrison gives the character more life than the screenplay does, yet both she and Beckwith seem to collaborate on the film's final image, which - like much of this odd, daring, and surprisingly resonant film - lands with a light touch upon hard matters.

Sweet, sensitive and surprisingly insightful, Nikole Beckwith's "Together Together" fashions the signposts of the romantic comedy - the meet-cute, the misunderstanding, the mutual acceptance - into a wry examination of a very different relationship.
A delightfully undemanding film that will put a huge smile on your face.
It's an ode to the way that even impermanent relationships can be profoundly meaningful.
This is a small, simple story, free from emotional pyrotechnics and, mostly, false notes.
The high points - and there are several - make the film worthwhile viewing, especially a breathtaking finale that will linger in the minds of those who watch.
It doesn't have the predictable, tidy feeling like a lot of films of this nature. It's quite appealing and charming.

title: Tom Clancy's Without Remorse | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Without Remorse follows a compelling protagonist in a path of revenge through suspenseful, intense action sequences triggered by the usual cliches and storytelling formulas of the genre. Michael B. Jordan is the star of the show.
Tom Clancy's Without Remorse may give you a case of buyer’s remorse.
Jordan sells it all with intensity and ferocity to spare. He leaves us wanting more which is a good thing considering the mid-credits scene we get.
Nearly everything about this film lands right in the middle. The action isn't bad, as much as it's just fine. The story isn't necessarily poor either; it's just mediocre.
Well placed in the streaming queue when you need a break from complicated miniseries or Oscar hopefuls.
Stefano Sollimas latest film moves like a well-oiled machine that stands as a solid, if a little flawed, Clancy adaptation.
Jordan carries as much weight as his well muscled back can hold but in the end Without Remorse lacks ingenuity, sincerity, and meaning.
As generic as they come. The film equivalent of a computer blackout screen.

Without Remorse proves watchable and mindlessly harmless, which may give it a second life as the start of a franchise. If screenwriters give the character Kelly more range, Jordan has the skill and charm to make him a hero worth watching again.
All the slow-burning cinematography in the world can't disguise that Without Remorse is assembled almost entirely from creaky spy/action movie cliches.
Jordan offers here a unique work that nevertheless works perfectly. [Full Review in Spanish]
To paraphrase the immortal Regina George, maybe Hollywood should stop trying to make Tom Clancy happen.

Sollima brings a dark visual intensity to the film, and the action sequences work on their own merit, but still fail to bring the various strands of the narrative together in an emotionally compelling way

"Without Remorse" is all about the action (nothing enlightening about global politics) and the action set pieces will hold your attention, as will the charismatic, physical specimen Michael B. Jordan-ditto for Jodie Turner-Smith.
Without Remorse isn't necessarily a great action film, but it is a delicious throwback to a time when a sturdy shoot-em-up was its own reward.
It's an all-around fail from a writer, director and star on a number of disappointing levels, refusing to light the fuse for an explosive and thrilling offering.
...dour, grim, and intensely forgettable.
This is incredibly boring. Very generic story. With such a great cast, this was very disappointing.
Some of the action was good. But the movie as a whole is very forgettable but that's not Michael B. Jordan's fault.
Michael B. Jordan excels in this latest Tom Clancy thriller. Without Remorse is a welcome addition to the super spy, soldier-gone-rogue universe

title: Things Heard & Seen | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's all crushingly predictable, advancing along the expected lines without even the slightest hint of something extra or new.
Well-cast and often entertaining but campy and sometimes obvious.
"Please stop with the ghost stuff," a character asks in Netflix misfire Things Heard & Seen, a request the film is conflicted about.
Overwrought horror starring an overqualified cast.
It's got good bones... But the movie itself winds up so blah.

You know a ghost story is a hot mess when it strands a stellar Amanda Seyfried and a top cast in a remote, country house haunted by toxic masculinity, dangling plot threads and nothing worth hearing or seeing.

It's hard to write about how all this happens without tarnishing the effect, but eventually you feel it building, taking its time, shining light on previous details that might have led you to twiddle your thumbs.
At two hours, Things Heard & Seen could stretch the patience of even the most sedentary couch-surfer, who won't be happy to be rewarded by a denouement in which absolutely everything falls apart...
All of these familiar beats might have found some tension to build on if every character trait and plot turn weren't already so clumsily foreshadowed, or blatantly spelled out...

Catherine spends the first half of the film feeling trapped in a roomy yet empty space, wanting more and frustrated that she's not getting it - a feeling the viewer comes to sympathize with all too well.

Rather than interweaving domestic drama, supernatural mumbo-jumbo and campus naughtiness, Pulcini and Berman lurch from one scene to the next, squandering scares and undermining the momentum of the story.

[W]hile "Things Heard & Seen" is not in the same league as "A Quiet Place" and Charlie Kaufman's oddball Netflix thriller, it has a spooky atmosphere and an appealingly slow boil that will liven up a Saturday night.
Seyfried and Norton are believable as the couple at its center, and Berman and Pulcini paint them into a world that's beginning to crumble around them.

The emphasis on Catherine puzzling out the house's past grows tedious... and while Seyfried acquits herself and then some, an actor of her talent is wasted on a character that spends most of the movie just connecting the dots.
But while the cast is great, the milieu is vivid, the images are polished and the atmosphere is effectively moody, "Things Heard & Seen" fails to connect on a visceral level.

This half-baked chiller disintegrates in a nonsensical finale that makes you want to slap your forehead in disgust. It's really too bad since Norton gives such a tremendously calculated performance and other individual elements work so well.
[Things Heard & Seen] boasts a fantastic cast of actors who are always fascinating to watch even when the material itself is less so.

Berman and Pulcini's failure to generate suspense becomes problematic during a second half that settles into standard psycho-spouse thriller rhythms with some half-assed ghost-story and feminist elements tossed in.

Like many Netflix originals, Things Heard And Seen is the cinematic equivalent of a mass-market paperback, neither good enough to haunt the viewer nor bad enough to haunt the résumés of its cast and crew.
Adapting Elizabeth Brundage's novel All Things Cease to Appear (a better title), the co-directors craft a surprisingly unusual ghost story that lingers.

title: The Guardian (2006) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A simple, predictable, and formulaic action flick.
The Guardian is ultimately a by the numbers movie that failed to hit big at the box office, seemingly lost to time. Various elements seem dated or unintentionally hilarious.

When I left the theater, it was with not only newfound knowledge and respect for the men and women of our Coast Guard, but with a wave of excitement from the sheer excellence and entertainment of the film.
As tiresome as it is drawn out.

There's nothing particularly wrong with it, it's just very tedious. Originality doesn't seem to be important and maybe it doesn't have to be as The Guardian is dealing with something true but what that something is the filmmakers seem to know.
"The Guardian" is a pro-military propaganda movie from Hollywood that attempts to mask its agenda behind the life-saving rhetoric of Coast Guard rescue swimmers.
There is a breadth of quality about the acting, including a fine performance from Sela Ward as Ben's estranged wife - making a lot more of her role than her meagre scripting suggests.
Overly bloated action drama that is predictable and drawn out.
Will definitely rescue some moviegoers from the post-summer doldrums, but someone should have told Davis that there's going to be casualities if he leaves audiences in the water that long.
The Guardian isn't as boring as Annapolis and SWAT, but it's still a feature-length training montage about kids learning the importance of taking it to the limit.
...an old-fashioned, irresistibly earnest piece of work...
A well-judged performance by Kevin Costner brings drama to this actioner.
I'd have given it an A-. But it goes on & on, off the deep end into the even hokier. But since it choked me up earlier on, I'm calling it a weak B .
The Guardian is an ordinary movie about extraordinary people.
This character-driven drama about redemption feels fresh, mostly due to good storytelling and two fine lead performances
a drama that's sometimes as generic as its title... (but)when they're not being forced to snarl at each other, Costner and Kutcher make a likable team...
full review in Greek
The film certainly comes across like a paid Coast Guard advertisement at times.

title: The Virtuoso | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Lethargic direction and bland acting drags down what could have been a decent neo-noir.
Michael Caine famously bought a new house with his fee for making Jaws 4. What Anthony Hopkins splashed out on after completing The Virtuoso remains unknown.
Too dumb to actually be any good and too dull to at least be entertainingly bad.
This is a committedly mediocre movie. The script reads like a rough draft that should be gathering dust.
"The Virtuoso" covers well-worn territory - the assassin story is almost a genre unto itself - and director Nick Stagliano, hampered by a predictable script, can't bring much new to the game.
When it's all over and the big twist you saw coming in the first 15 minutes has been revealed, you feel empty, a bit depressed, and like you need another cup of coffee.
"The Virtuoso," directed by Nick Stagliano from a script by James C. Wolf, misses its shot in a spectacular, and sometimes spectacularly pretentious, fashion.
Making the best of a shabby job? Funnily enough, even if it all too rarely heeds its own brief, that's what The Virtuoso is all about.
Hopkins isn't awful in "The Virtuoso," but the movie that surrounds him is.
The payoff makes sense, but it delivers far less than intended.

title: Four Good Days | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Perhaps the most fascinating aspect of this shallow movie is left unexplored: why doesn't Deb look in the mirror at her role in Molly's addiction?
Mila Kunis does her finest acting work alongside Glenn Close...
It is a couple of good performances in a movie that feels like we have seen it a thousand times before.

The subject matter will certainly resonate for many, but even with its fact-based underpinnings Four Good Days feels like a bit of a Frankenstein monster, stitched together from past addiction movies.
Character actor Stephen Root, 69, plays the largely understanding stepfather in this contemporary tearjerker released in the shadow of the Oscar-nominated Hillbilly Elegy.
These are important stories that should be seen, but audiences need more than scripts that are primarily acting exercises.
What sets "Four Good Days" apart from the many other films of its ilk are Close and Kunis, who sharpen and elevate its well-worn contours with vivid performances that are honest and grounded.
Scene by scene, Close and Kunis drag us into their family problems, and we end up caring.
"Four Good Days" is more complex than its outward trappings and preachier scenes - like an anguished Molly addressing a high school class - suggest.
[C]o-writer and director Rodrigo García (who worked with Close on "Albert Nobbs") knows where to keep his focus and how to frame his story.
Both Glenn Close and Mila Kunis are very talented actors, but Four Good Days gives them absolutely nothing interesting to say or do.
Still, "Four Good Days" nails what addiction is like for the afflicted and those who love them. Close and Kunis work well together.
"Four Good Days" could be a better movie, but I'm not sure that matters.
Though this agonizing weeklong ordeal reaches a shrill climax, the denouement feels rushed, opaque, leaving us only with more questions.
Four Good Days doesn't have much to offer to the audience, except for an occasionally effective Glenn Close.
Even with two strong lead performances, "Four Good Days" feels awfully well-worn.
As a performer's showcase, "Four Good Days" does the job. But there's not much to see here otherwise.

Persuasively acted, compassionately observed and thoroughly unsurprising, this is well-intentioned material that never quite gets beyond its inspired-by-a-true-story, issue-driven TV movie-of-the-week template.
"Four Good Days" is based on a true story, and the way it plays out is both watchable and plausible. Yet the movie doesn't shake us to our souls.

title: Those Who Wish Me Dead | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Those Who Wish Me Dead wants to be a neo-western with a heart, but its damaged heroes are straight from the cliche playbook.

Those Who Wish Me Dead has a tendency to veer into the over-sentimental and it has an ending that is heart-on-its-sleeve earnest. But this taut, contained story with well-directed action is as an effective thriller.

It's very very by the numbers, ticking all the genre boxes, and the cliches sometimes become too much, but it is what it is as popcorn entertainment doing a lot of subversive things around the edges...
Those Who Wish Me Dead ends up offering something quite radical within its understated package.
It was far-fetched and there were lots of plot holes.
This is a really well-meaning, predictable, attempting-to-have-an-emotional-hook action movie that just didn't work well.
That grounding in reality helps "Those Who Wish Me Dead" stand out, and it's backed by a solid, straightforward game of cat and mouse.
Sheridan's flair has always been in ensembles, but here that trait is caught in a stalemate with the desire to provide an underwhelming Jolie with a star vehicle.
Those Who Wish Me Dead could have risen to meet Jolie's ability. But the film reflects the industry's lack of imagination for an older female action star.
Unfortunately, the second half is over-reliant on flashy disaster set pieces, blazing towards a predictable, melodramatic conclusion.

Angelina Jolie continues her seemingly unstoppable run as a gifted film director (see First They Killed My Father) who makes terrible choices in front of the camera by following the execrable Come Away with this preposterous mishmash thriller.

The fiery explosions and chase sequences are handsomely shot, but the plot is undeniably absurd and the ominous/rousing soundtrack downright hokey. It's the performances and banter that make the project worth watching.
"Those Who Wish Me Dead" has an awfully twee title. It comes from Michael Koryta's 2014 novel. But the twee-ness is OK, since this adaptation is pretty good, if also violent and a bit overblown.
But sometimes you simply want to see a movie star stab a guy in the chest while a raging inferno burns in the background. Even if it's not August.
"Those Who Wish Me Dead" - an enjoyable, absorbing, characterful testament to shuffling the whole deck of genre conventions, and then politely setting it on fire.

Angelina Jolie, back in action mode as a haunted smokejumper seeking redemption, gets the job done if you're looking for action escapism, but those who wish for something deeper and more resonant are out of luck.
The contours of this story, and the tinges of genuine melancholy thrown into our path along the way, are very much to the point. They make it all work, and make it worth it.
Angelina Jolie's bare-knuckled performance in Those Who Wish Me Dead easily outclasses the film that contains it.
If Sheridan's film is meant to convey the long stretches of boredom before brief moments of excitement, it succeeds.

A lean, engrossing, action-packed shot of adrenaline that is striking in its aesthetic decisions and boasts some exceedingly fun turns from its actors. Most important, it proves once more why Jolie is a star.

title: Mainstream | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Once "Mainstream" locks into its purpose - showing the vapidity, cruelty and calculation of certain YouTube stars - it soars.
A more incisive film would have something to say about using empty spectacle to comment on empty spectacle.
[Mainstream] drills down hard into its subject, jettisoning Coppola's previous restraint in favor of a more confrontational and graceless hyperactivity.
The film has the knowing swagger of something on the cutting edge but none of the self-awareness to realize it's late to the party.
A horrifically empty "social media satire"...
Mainstream takes a while (and a lot of hipster costume changes) to get there, but it eventually throws up some pertinent questions to ponder...
A big, blunt, sanctimonious satire of YouTuber idolatry that, for all its bug-eyed, pin-balling energy, never feels remotely ahead of the curve.
It's a messy, childish scrawl of a film, but it is high on energy.
Mainstream never transcends the impasse of being another update of the old story about hipster radicals challenging the system only to be devoured by it...

The plot is just as predictable as the themes. Everyone watching will know where it's going, although the viewer's imagined version of the screenplay will likely be shrewder than the one written by Coppola and Tom Stuart.
Soon becomes the very thing it sets out to expose: a glittery, jangly image machine that manufactures little of actual substance, except the conclusion that social media = bad.
Mainstream is a cautionary tale to approach with caution, deserving of a like but perhaps not quite a subscribe.

title: Finding You | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Even as an amorous daydream, "Finding You" is dated and generic, Disney Channel-movie-esque, but without the charismatic teen stars.
Scores around six on the logarithmic PH scale - Paddywhackery Hazard - that leads from acceptable neo-realist films at one to the herb we won't mention again at 10.
Tiny specks of grit get entirely smoothed over in pearlescent sentimentality by the end, eased through by lashings of flute-and-fiddle noodlings on the soundtrack.
[T]here's not much here outside of glossy stargazing and fluffy daydreams, except for the exquisite greenery of Ireland. That's so real you couldn't fake it if you tried.
It's as if Finding You was written by a computer program that studied 2000s rom-coms, taking the worst tropes and clunkily blending them together.

A rom-com (with splashes of drama, care of death, cancer, and the price of celebrity, surely all stellar romantic hallmarks) that never met a contrivance it didn't love, right down to its winking take on "Notting Hill."
If you like rom-coms, this will win your heart.
But the film forgot to graft a personality onto its protagonist and seems so determined to be PG-clean that sparks between the leads are ... hard to "find."
A not-insignificant miscalculation aside, effervescent performances from an ebullient ensemble make Finding You a palatable and compelling female coming-of-age tale.
It would never work, Finley warns us, and it seems she might as well be talking about this cornball movie. But thanks to something ineffable... "Finding You" kinda, sorta does.

title: The Woman in the Window | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A clockwork noir of diabolical determinism.
A strong and decidedly suspenseful murder melodrama.
The Woman in the Window is mostly notable as a dry run for the following year's Scarlet Street.
It's not merely a dazzling piece of suspense, but also a characteristically stark demonstration of Lang's belief in the inevitability of fate.
The Woman in the Window is a humdinger of a mystery melodrama.
A masterful film noir from Fritz Lang's rich American period.

title: Army of the Dead | Rotten Tomatoes
Spirit Untamed | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is family entertainment that's quite niche in its appeal - pony-mad kids will love it, but it may test the patience of parents.
It'll pass the time easily enough for young viewers, but everyone else will wish they were spirited away on a more sophisticated adventure.
The girl-power message works fine, but the original movie's lesson about wildness being the true nature of animals is gone.
A smaller studio collaborated with Dreamworks this time and the animation is all CGI. But once the girls take off on their quest, the momentum takes over and you forget about the niceties.
I can picture the 10-year-old girls at a slumber party for whom this movie would be the biggest hit, and I hope their parents rent it for them.
Spirit Untamed wasn't a horse I found a lot of enjoyment in riding.
"Spirit Untamed" lacks spirit, and even worse, it lacks soul.

Spirit Untamed is pure and unbridled family fun, pardon the pun. The animation is crisp and light, the voice performances are crackling good and the story of Spirit and the girl who became his best friend is filled with heart.
Spirit Untamed never seems to know which trail it's taking.
An exciting, heartwarming story and co-writer/co-director Elaine Bogan has a perceptive understanding of the vital importance of the P-A-L (the girls' initials) friendship.
The characters have the rudimentary appearance of people in a carpeting commercial, as if animators planned to take a couple more passes to add shading and depth but forgot to do so.
More like "Spirit Uninteresting."
"Spirit Untamed" takes full advantage of Merced's range and has some finely drawn characters, but the story is rather threadbare.
A harmless animated adventure that will provide a bland diversion to young viewers.
The kiddies, I'm sure, will be satisfied.
The scenery of wind-and water-eroded mesas and stone archways is lovely, but the voice performances are largely inert and unremarkable.

Feels more suited for repeat living room watches, rather than a big-screen movie theater event. However, "Spirit Untamed" is a sweet film with a moving message about embracing family, heritage and most importantly, yourself, just the way you are.
While the message of Spirit Untamed is a good one...it's hard not to see the movie as an easy money grab.
Perfectly serviceable for younger audiences, particularly those with an affinity for horses, it never quite soars beyond a run-of-the-mill story.
The film still can't compare to the one that started this franchise, but families could do far worse when it comes to wholesome entertainment.

title: Blast Beat | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's grounded in sincere emotion and very thoughtful in its exploration of the American Dream.
The film wants to talk about so many topics, and yet it ends up shortchanging all of them so that it can make for one massive emotional scene after the next.
"Blast Beat" powers through its clichés by cranking up a soundtrack of Synapticide and the Eastside Boyz.
There's plenty of potential here to bring original insights to the immigrant experience, but not enough skill in the plotting or execution to tap into it.
A terrific bilingual debut that keenly scrutinizes the American Dream, those who pursue it vehemently, and the ones who reject it as the sole avenue to fulfillment.

title: Dream Horse | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is a small, sentimental and straightforward film that offers little in the way of surprises. Instead, it wins on heart and a simple message about the value in fighting to keep one's dreams alive.
"Hywl" is a Welsh word that is described on-screen as a "feeling of emotional motivation and energy" - and Dream Horse has certainly imbued its likeable story with plenty of "hwyl".
This is a character-driven movie and the horse is not the main character...

It's a story with all the hallmarks of a typically British feel-good movie in the tradition pioneered by the Ealing comedies of the post-WWII years when the country needed all the laughs it could raise.
The feelgood Brit-com is back!
Shamelessly predictable and thoroughly feelgood.
What it lacks in originality, it makes up for in the sheer force of its sincerity.
Its saving grace is a wonderful - and convincingly accented - lead performance by Toni Collette...

Dream Horse is predictable and manipulative to a fault but, sparked by Toni Collette, there is a strong sense of sincerity and commitment to the subject matter that helps it across the finishing line.
The resulting movie may be a bit schmaltzy - actually, a lot schmaltzy - but I couldn't help enjoying it: like Chariots of Fire, only with horses.
I didn't find any great pleasure in seeing a story play out [the way] I knew exactly how it was going to play out.
It's super cheesy and formulaic, but it is also a total crowdpleaser. If you like that kind of film... I think it really fits the bill.
Poetic licence nudges forward backstories of marital strife, but the film's touch is deft. Likewise, the comedy of small-town eccentrics, rowdily played without tipping into snobbery.
Toni Collette is a sure thing in Dream Horse, a thoroughly predictable but ultimately winning underdog sports movie.
While there's nothing remarkable or surprising about this movie from director Euros Lyn and screenwriter Neil McKay, it's nearly impossible to dislike.
The racetrack tale's uplifting story, heartwarming moments and beautiful scenery pay off in a big way.

Sure it's hokey, but this fact-based crowdpleaser starring a terrific Toni Collette as a struggling Welsh villager who risks everything on a racehorse she breeds and raises is an underdog story that works like a charm.
Sit back, let your resting pulse rate slow to an easy Acorn crawl, and watch Collette and Co.'s sweetly scrappy dream come true.
Watching the film navigate... clichés has a special satisfaction. It's like watching Dream clear the fences in the Grand National at Aintree.
It feels familiar because of its clichés, but it's a rousing enough story that those clichés don't hold it back from making an impact. Plain and simple, Dream Horse just works.

title: A Quiet Place Part II | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Krasinski's instincts are very good, and once you've placed the primary action there...then it allows the story to move forward, maintain and even build on the tension of the original.
"More of the same" has rarely been carried off with such elan.
The characters ooze slowly and lethargically away from each other, and without that farmhouse location, and the symbolic power of the family it implies, the horror movie tension simply evaporates.
Krasinski's slick, skilful follow-up to his 2018 post-apocalyptic thriller works well as a genre exercise...
While it's not as fresh or surprising as the original, A Quiet Place Part II adeptly balances the demands of both the genre movie and the emotional impact of the family drama.
Maybe nothing could have possibly matched the original for me. [But] everyone is very good in it. The kids, Noah Jupe and Millicent Simmonds, really are the stars here.

The new film has inevitably lost the concision of the last, in the same way the minimalist frights of Alien were swapped for the wham-bam action of Aliens... In other instances, though, the stakes have been raised.
If you haven't been unsettled enough in the past year, A Quiet Place Part II is just the thing.
There's a great benefit to seeing a movie that depends for much of its impact on a brilliant soundtrack with long passages of silence and an appreciative audience.
The Abbotts venture into the unknown in a meticulously crafted monster movie that leaves us wanting more.

While it is certainly thrilling for its duration, what you see - or hear - is what you get. For here, as in A Quiet Place, viewers will find little subtext to keep ringing and resonating in their ears afterwards.
The true talent of A Quiet Place Part II belongs to editor Michael P. Shawver, who manages to turn two relatively straightforward storylines into competing narratives tied to a singular outcome.
Apart from such cliches, there doesn't seem to be much going on in A Quiet Place Part II - or if there is, nobody's talking.
I never lost track of what was occurring where or to whom, tension rising incrementally with such violent intensity it almost became unbearable.

Krasinski presents these and other such details with lucidity. His direction is so efficient and assured that the three or four rather ridiculous plot elements go unnoticed until well after the movie's over. That's how absorbing "Part II" can be.
There are nitpicks - some small, some a little bigger - but mostly, "A Quiet Place Part II" does its job by giving viewers more and leaving them wanting even more. That's the modern franchise way.
All I could think about was Marc Maron's go-to jab on WTF when talking about comics he doesn't appreciate: "It's like math" ... It's so tightly crafted that the filmmaking is almost oppressive.
I'd recommend it to horror fans even if the COVID-19 pandemic had never happened, but I can't think of a more fitting way to return to movie theaters.

A Quiet Place Part IIdeserves to succeed because it's so good-not just because it's coasting on an earlier hit. Like any sequel it can't offer a fresh core concept...but it can extend the thrills and chills without seeming forced or contrived
A lopsided film, one whose returns ever diminish toward another sudden ending.

title: Aquarium of the Dead | Rotten Tomatoes
The Conjuring: The Devil Made Me Do It | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: I watched this with my 16-year-old son and we liked it, peeking through our fingers and laughing in equal measure.
With its third-act stumbles, it never quite catches either The Conjuring or The Conjuring 2, but it proves there is still spirit left in this franchise.
The biographical nuts and bolts are intriguing and, as ever, the jump scares and murk are professionally timed and delivered.
It's disappointing to stop rooting for a blockbuster behemoth horror series, but The Conjuring movies' quality and talon-tight hold has rapidly deflated over time.

I don't find these films frightening, but the Warrens as a couple -- with their daffy, retro updos that look quasi-Victorian and Brady Bunch -- have grown on me by this point. They're just dorky, and I like watching them hang out.
The film apes the style that James Wan established with the original Conjuring without establishing any real identity of its own.
With two more spinoffs currently in development, it's clear that the producers' prayers have been answered. But me, I'm still agnostic.
This third trip into the horrifying unknown with Ed and Lorraine Warren is a tedious bit of supernatural déjà vu.
The thrill is gone. The fun has died. The point is blunted and yet more dangerous. So, don't be tempted by The Conjuring: The Devil Made Me Do It.
The franchise descends deeper into the bowels of silliness.
"The Conjuring: The Devil Made Me Do It" is a fine installment but in an increasingly creaky franchise, appropriate for films that adore the sound of rotting wood floors.
The terror of losing oneself to a demon or, in the case of Lorraine Warren, to a psychic reconstruction of such a possession, is worthy of all the rattles the film inspires.
It's not Chaves's takeover that makes this new film feel like it runs off the rails - it's the choice to shift focus from a haunting to a murder.

The third and weakest chapter in the "Conjuring" series messes with the facts about a real-life case of demonic possession as a legal defense, but Farmiga and Wilson as married demonologists know how to marshall nerve-rattling chills.
What's compelling about "Devil" is how the Warrens remain united in faith and love.
The devil made me watch it!
Fatigue has caught up with the Warrens, and the question about the franchise is not where it can go from here, but how much longer it can be sustained by humdrum deviltry.
The big set-pieces where the demon emerges from hiding rely on the usual devices: rattles and roars, frantic camera work and flashing lights.
Despite the weakness of the conclusions they draw, Chaves still finds room for a few classic Conjuring scares...

Before it loses its damn mind halfway through, the latest in the Conjuring Universe franchise holds up decently enough with its atmosphere and gotcha scares. Ultimately, however, it doesn't cast a convincing spell.

title: Cruella | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: These clothes are the boldest element of a movie that otherwise wears its supposed punk-rock influences like a kid discovering Hot Topic for the first time.
This movie is worth watching for how it looks and sounds and for Emma Thompson...
Cruella is doing enough to be seductively fun and entertaining, at least for the first 90 minutes.
The movie is fun, stylish, and over the top (in mostly a good way), but it struggles to prove that it's more than a muddled cash grab.

Cruella is often fun to watch, but its cavalier reversal of its core character cheapens the very idea of a corrective narrative. It takes a quintessential villain and nuances her character into oblivion.
This becomes repetitive and one-note after you get past how deliciously wicked everyone is.
Very funny, and when we consider how easy it would've been to completely drop the ball, the fact that it's fun is seriously underrated...Thompson just sets the screen on fire.

Although this film is not for me and struggles to hit 2/5, the 10-year-old I saw it with was so tickled by it and explicitly instructed me to note in this review that they give it a 4/5. So in the spirit of democracy, a 3/5 it is
The Met Gala should be so lucky.
Cruella is not as perfect as the seams Estella stitches, but there's something ever so charming about its strut.

Stone's performance slips into high gear, reaching an entertainingly manic level. There's a crazed glint in her eye that is more than a match for Thompson's basilisk stare, and Gillespie's design department backs her up.
That Cruella is an atrocity with neither purpose nor soul shouldn't come as a surprise.
Stone is a joy: vampy, sneering and as eager to please as a dalmatian.
There's not much of One Hundred and One Dalmatians author Dodie Smith's source material or its classic 1961 animated adaptation to be found inside Disney's Cruella, and I'm perfectly okay with that.
A film doesn't need pretty costumes to be enjoyable, but it does need good storytelling-which is the missing ingredient in Cruella.
When it counts, Craig Gillespie's blockbuster proves delicious.

"From the very beginning I've always made a statement," Cruella announces at the outset in voice-over. Very true, and the movie that bears her name makes statements of its own - a lot of them. It just can't decide which ones matter
It's just unfortunate that the muscular legacy of Cruella should, for now, end like this. Without a hint of cruelty at all.

Beavan's costumes are dazzling throughout, including Cruella's glittering red dress at the Baroness's gala. But when the costumes overwhelm the characters and story, there's something hollow at the film's centre.
At two-plus hours, "Cruella" could use a few trims. But as a mood board, it's a smashing success.

title: Dutch | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's all assembly-line stuff.
If a film like this is to be funny at all, it had better work when the warring principals still hate each other, before the rich boy is shown to be a sweet kid and the whole story turns to mush.
Simply a tired, predictable retread of plot snippets and hollow characters from previous Hughes productions.
Hughes, a man more prolific than Stephen King and less inspired than Aaron Spelling, has produced yet another forgettable project. This movie shouldn't even be allowed on planes.
Hughes has written, directed and/or produced so many of these films by now that perhaps we can even forgive him for beginning to repeat himself.
The acting is only a little more uninspired than the screenplay, which is directed without shame or flair by Peter Faiman of Crocodile Dundee.

title: Under the Stadium Lights | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: "Under the Stadium Lights" makes no effort to comprehend larger societal and systemic forces; it preaches grit, gumption, and a docile, unquestioning compassion.
Under the Stadium Lights is pee wee by comparison to Peter Berg's All-American.

Though this one doesn't equal the genre's gold standard -- Denzel Washington's Remember the Titans -- the audience can rely on multiple adversity-crushing character arcs, the inevitable Gipper speech and the rousing big-game finale.
It fails to reach for an audience outside of its world.
Between long stretches of TV clips from real-life games, ponderous melodrama unfolds.
Occasional clips of the original games are presented with so little context they seem designed to jog memories rather than advance the drama.

title: Gully | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The plot here didn't work for me, but I really adore this cast and I think this director will make something great.
A movie... needs to go somewhere, and "Gully" basically doesn't.
Uncertain what story it's telling, Nabil Elderkin's Gully is only held together by the sheer talent of its young cast.
The film overreaches or overstates at every significant moment...
Its raw, gritty approach feels like an effort from the filmmakers, but it's mostly work for the audience to endure.
Music video director Nabil Elderkin steps into the deep end of feature filmmaking and flounders.

title: Grace and Grit | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: For a metaphysical love-conquers-all tale, "Grace and Grit" offers very little substance around such lofty concepts as existence, spirituality and romantic harmony.
If you can make it through the first ten minutes of "Grace and Grit" without groaning, then your tolerance for New Age folderols, saccharin voice-overs and seraphic gazes is higher than mine.

title: Queen Bees | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Director Michael Lembeck handles it all with an anonymous efficiency.
It's a film that seems to have been dreamt up by a reverent grandchild who assumed they knew everything there was to know and never thought to ask the grandparent themselves.
An ideal date night or friends' group evening out. Love is love and there's no expiration date. Or, as Curtin's bossy biddy says, tongue planted firmly in cheek, "Eighty is the new 18."
Half a dozen veteran performers do their best to elevate a patchy script in Queen Bees, a gentle romantic comedy set in a retirement community.
A middling comedy that plays like it was underwritten by the Retirement Community Association of America, if there were such a thing.
For all the superficiality and shortcomings of "Queen Bees," the film's biggest draw, and strongest attribute, is its packed ensemble of iconic actors.
The writing and directing are highly uneven, but "Queen Bees" is made generally watchable by a veritable Who's Who of vintage talent.
Michael Lembeck's genial, predictable comedy rolls along on well-worn tracks elevated by the class and commitment of actors who've earned our affection over decades of work.
"Queen Bees" is a milquetoast affair, akin to an extended "Golden Girls" episode, only with a little more drama and a lot less wit.
Each of these stalwarts bring more than charisma to their roles, and when the writing itself displays some snap (which admittedly isn't that often) the performers bite right into it.
Ellen Burstyn and James Caan head an unusually strong cast of familiar faces in director Michael Lembeck's indie crowd-pleaser.

title: The House Next Door: Meet the Blacks 2 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Any potential is lost within the time the film spends bleeding out cheap cliches.

title: Fathom | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: What a shame.

title: Rita Moreno: Just a Girl Who Decided to Go For It | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Hollywood still has much work to do, but Moreno rightly gets her flowers.

Overall, she emerges just as vampish, feisty and fun as you'd expect, and as a gracious giver of speeches at ceremonies where she collects endless lifetime achievement awards, her biggest side-hustle next to acting.
The documentary is rich in archival clips, but mostly it's just rich in her -- and Moreno is tons of fun.
Director Mariem Pérez Riera never gets in the way of her subject and lets viewers feel Moreno's spirit, her vibrancy and her energy.

Even in a film that makes no bones about presenting its subject in a flattering, softening light, this 89-year-old stage and screen legend has refreshingly few qualms about saying exactly what she thinks.

The new documentary Rita Moreno: Just A Girl Who Decided To Go For It reiterates many of those anecdotes, but it doesn't tell us much that Moreno hasn't divulged already in her 2013 memoir or in countless interviews over the years.

The film, anchored by interviews with Moreno and her co-stars and contemporaries, positions Moreno as a trailblazer, a barrier-breaker, and a role model, but more interestingly, it ultimately tracks a journey of self discovery.

A fascinating and at times sobering look at [Moreno's] romances, and her personal struggles with self-esteem and self-worth, as well as the racism, misogyny, and sexual abuse she endured throughout her seven-decade career.
Like everything else she's done, Rita Moreno is an exceptional storyteller, turning Rita Moreno: Just a Girl Who Decided to Go For It into a dazzling look at the much-adorned star's career.
If there's an award for straight-to-the-camera performance, Ms. Moreno's appearance here should win it by acclamation.
A funny, occasionally foul-mouthed and almost startlingly frank portrait...
Moreno, now in her late 80s, thoughtfully walks us through a life that encompassed both enormous success and constant struggle.
It's almost hard to believe that the radiant Moreno we see in the film - who at 89 continues to epitomize that ineffable and rare quality we call star power - was ever restrained.
What truly sets the movie apart is Moreno's unwavering honesty.
One of the most satisfying things about the film is that through decades of struggle she clearly has found that worth.
A couple of things that stand out in the excellent new documentary "Rita Moreno: A Girl Who Decided to Go for It" is that the Berkeley resident is ferocious - and oh so vulnerable.
Riera mercifully doesn't wallow in West Side Story, and instead shares Moreno's power as an activist and an EGOT-winning performer who continues to break barriers as an 87-year-old...
It makes you feel both the highs and lows of being such a trailblazer in Hollywood.
Closer to home is Rita Moreno: Just a Girl Who Decided to Go For It, a long-overdue tribute to the Puerto Rican actress...
Rita Moreno's glow, as she reveals secrets, speaks her truths and revels in her glory, elevates this very standard bio/doc.

title: Love Spreads | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The lines are lightly humorous, while the pacing is deliberately frustrated... The one disappointment is the music that emerges in the final act. It’s beyond bland and hardly worth the agony. Although this, possibly, could be the point.

title: 12 Mighty Orphans | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Who could resist a Depression-era sports drama involving Texas orphans and a gentle, do-gooder head football coach named Rusty Russell?
It's an up-from-struggle story tailor-made for an old-fashioned, family-friendly, earnest, feel-good movie, and that's exactly what Roberts delivers,
12 Mighty Orphans and 1,200 not-so-mighty clichés.
"12 Mighty Orphans" tries so hard to be inspirational that it trips itself up on its way out to the field. Great story, but the telling is second-string.
"12 Mighty Orphans" is a feel-good football film. It's just not very good. But at times, it is good enough.
Nothing that happens in "12 Mighty Orphans" is unexpected, but these two pros still react with infectious wonder as the messages they send to their students take root and then sprout.
A plodding football drama in which the characters talk to one another like folksy social workers.
"12 Mighty Orphans" manages to subvert a few of the expected clichés to reasonably original effect, and the ensemble of lesser-known young actors is across-the-board strong.
If you're looking for an old-fashioned sports drama, this is it.
Even though there are moments of intense emotion and struggle, Roberts maintains a quiet, deliberate tone.
The story proceeds in expected melodramatic fashion.

Not a fan of football, but a fan of overcoing adversity , which is exactly what this "dirty dozen" orphans accomplish under the guidance of Rusty Russell. It's a feel good story delivered at exactly the right time

Football fans, or those longing for bygone days of old timey sayings and men with conventional character, may find enjoyment in the film's spelled out structure. Others will be at the mercy of its barrage of inspiration, devoid of insight.

The script is littered with misogynistic locker room talk, from the use of "ladies" as an insult, to immediately objectifying Vinessa Shaw, who plays Russell's wife Juanita, as soon as she appears on screen.

title: The Sparks Brothers | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: From bucket-of-water tomfoolery to visually inventive biography and witty musicology, this really does have something for the girl with everything.
The Sparks Brothers film is smart, funny, infectiously weird, a little geeky, a little too long, a little niche, and consistently entertaining.
The film is too long and, although Wright hopes it will convert heathens, it's still probably one for the fans. The Maels, however, make enjoyably unpredictable hosts.
Less a documentary than an intensive course of art-pop hypnotherapy: even those who enter the cinema knowing next to nothing about the pair will leave feeling like lifelong enthusiasts.
Wright presents an unabashed love letter to a band he clearly loves and does it with style, humour and great attention to detail.
Wright's film has converted me. Sparks are the Gilbert and George of pop music.
Canters joyfully through their biographies, pop history and - like all the best rock docs - an array of topics that intersect with the subject at hand.
A documentary of granular detail and depth that showcases Sparks in all their glorious, indefatigable absurdity, while leaving a clear mark of mystery.
Wright, whose features include Shaun of the Dead and Baby Driver, has made a terrifically informed and affectionate documentary about this duo.
So here we have Edgar Wright's thoroughly entertaining, if somewhat rambling, documentary about the brothers, and it's just as odd as you might hope but funnier than expected.
Wright successfully demystifies the enigma that is Sparks while adding to the mythology.
[Edgar Wright] is such a good filmmaker, and he's made a really fun, creatively challenging movie that's worth seeing whether you're a fan or not.
At its best, The Sparks Brothers courses with the energy of one of your smartest friends talking your ear off about their favorite band.
I am a newcomer to the Sparks phenomenon but now that I've seen Wright's new documentary The Sparks Brothers I'm a believer.
'The Sparks Brothers' makes you want to know them better.
"The Sparks Brothers" zips along at such a breezy, informational pace that you notice its length only in the final stretch, when the film's reduced to ticking off the albums as they keep coming.
Director Edgar Wright's documentary thoroughly recounts the siblings' 50-year career with help from admiring musicians and famous fans.
Disappointing might be a better word for it; one might have hoped that, when time came for Sparks to get their due, the treatment would better reflect the band's singularity.

Wright's debut documentary may seem a shift from his long career of modern screwball comedy, but he's almost accidentally perfect, channeling his own obsession with the understatedly quirky band into a pitch-perfect examination.
This film goes the distance with Sparks, spending almost as much time on the obscure later albums as the bestsellers.

title: False Positive | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's preaching in all caps. Or considering the oddly goofy tone, All Caps in Comic Sans.

It's the product of a satirical ambition that lacks the wit to land any heady blows; the horror mastery to be even glancingly scary; the intellect to make those thrills invigoratingly existential; and the sense of humor to make it entertaining.

False Positive doesn't sustain its most suspenseful ideas. The big revelation at the end is something of a letdown, and the movie's final image spells out a metaphor that ought to have been left to suggestion.
The movie, despite its weaknesses, has a heartbeat. It is frank about how frightening it is to ask for men's help when your body is on the line.
It all comes off as strangely enervating and flat-footed in the end: a story without a genre, or a point.

As the volume increases, the film's message distorts, and it starts grasping at too many different ideas that never cohere, abandoning subtext for wincingly on-the-nose exchanges that shatter the mood.
It's easy to forgive the deficiencies of False Positive, simply because it feels so oddly unique.
A valiant, but misguided, post-Get Out attempt to infuse social commentary within the framework of well-worn genre territory, aiming high but landing low.
There's a lot to wrestle with in "False Positive," but many of its issues seems to be that it's still be wrestling with itself.
With Ilana Glazer leading an outstanding cast, "False Positive" is not a movie you can easily shake off in a day or two. Or three.
Aspires to be a modern version of "Rosemary's Baby," but... ultimately lands somewhere between tepid and confused.
While "False Positive" has lapses in logic and could have a quicker pace in the second half, it fully embraces a bizarre sense of the macabre that is irresistible.
You won't be able to shake this one off.

"Perhaps the point of "False Positive" is that we cannot become inured to those all too-plausible villains who walk and work among us - and are applauded. They deserve our full-throated rage and bloodlust too."

The apparent desire by the core creative team to break from their wilder, messier material by giving False Positive A24 gloss and a steely Dead Ringers spine is understandable. But for a movie with this much blood, it doesn't leave much of a stain.
False Positive threads classic horror-film tropes with a woozy, partially comic sensibility but doesn't fully commit to this approach.
Misdirection abounds, from a series of strange nightmares to creepy visions of blood, but every "creepy" choice mostly registers as another cheap way to cover up a flagging narrative.

Despite the dark doings surrounding Lucy's pregnancy, it's the small observations that build the cornerstone of the film. Glazer wrote the script with her Broad City collaborator Lee, and they share a razor-sharp eye for the tiniest, most painful cuts.

It begins as a genre-bending tale about the perils of parenting. Then John Lee and Ilana Glazer take a hard left turn into something else so provocative, abstract, and ambitious that it's destined to become a conversation starter.
Clever, creepy and original enough to keep you glued.

title: The Birthday Cake | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Given its meandering script and absurdly grand guignol ending, it's astonishing that The Birthday Cake could attract such a starry cast.
No matter how you slice it, this star-studded mob film still seems undercooked.
Giannopoulos might be inexperienced, but he's canny with mood and unafraid to experiment with the rhythms of violence. I, for one, am keen to see what he does next.

title: Good on Paper | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: As an "anti-rom-com," hijacking the genre's rhythms without adhering to the rules of the game, Good on Paper is fine. As a satire of showbiz vapidity, it's decent. It's not nearly as subversive as you want it to be.
Shlesinger makes an engaging lead, charismatic and thought-provoking if not often laugh-out-loud funny.
Iliza Schlesinger takes a familiar premise and spins it with stand-up comedy reminding girls sometimes what is good on paper is a hot buttered mess waiting to be exposed
As a stand-up routine it may have worked, but some material is best left to the stage.
In her directorial debut, comedian Kimmy Gatewood handles the brittle material well, but it is the screenplay and the actors who make it a squirmingly good comedy.
Despite the movie's darker aspects, Gatewood and Shlesinger escape with some decent laughs and pointed questions.
Containing razor-sharp witticisms about feminine intuition, gendered sexual politics and relationships, it excels beyond its self-deprecating title.
It's a bravura portrayal of a character who's endearing, awkward and strange, in a movie that's definitely overlong but can be engagingly weird.
By the end, our sympathies lie with neither duper nor the duped.

Shlesinger's resistance to buffering over her prickly bits is the best thing about "Good on Paper." But that same care isn't applied to the rest of the film, which can never strike a balance with its many ideas and tones...
A witty tale of deceit and betrayal, it's an uncomfortable look at the values we tend to buy into and why.
Schlesinger's comedy also gets a little too smoothed out in the process, the film playing it safe when we want it to run wild.
In trying to both score laughs and impart a moral, Good On Paper doesn't really manage to do either; it's not funny enough to work as a straight comedy and not human enough to work as a dramedy.

title: Lansky | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: After so many Cosa Nostrums out of Hollywood tending to suggest that however violent, mobsters are also cute -- picking up tips from previous films on how to patter and swag; doing the Tarantino -- it's a relief to hear them in their brute banality.
What we are left with in ''Lansky'' is an affable buddy movie with aspirations, or maybe they are just affectations.

title: No Sudden Move | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Praise Soderbergh, and pass the ammunition.
This is a crime thriller with great acting that once again illustrates Steven Soderbergh's mastery of the genre.
"No Sudden Move" is a remarkably effervescent affair: not so much frothy as high-spirited, even when the story seems to be moving with the studied grace of a mime.

The intersection of criminal gangs and the American auto industry during the vast freeway expansion boom of the post-war years makes for fascinating bedfellows. And Soderbergh knows how to make the most of it.
A story about race and class and hidden pollution.
It's well-crafted and thrilling in a way that feels oddly reassuring.
Slouch back and enjoy the prolific Soderbergh's 35th movie. It might not move you straight away. By the end, though, you'll be buzzing.
The performances are unanimously on point. Even in his weaker movies Soderbergh seems incapable of drawing out a single substandard line-reading from his ensembles.

No Sudden Move has something different from the crackerjack noir swagger a younger director might have brought. Decades since his Out of Sight prime, Soderbergh invests it with a deluxe sense of fatigue.
A grown-up film that credits you with the brains to enjoy not knowing everything at once.
We all are in the river. Some of us are strong swimmers, some of us are not, and we have to decide whether to let the raft pass or climb aboard.
Bonus points for a regally menacing extended cameo by the great actor-director Bill Duke, who barely has to move (or speak) to impose his will on scenes.
Part of the fun of No Sudden Move is that we figure out what's going on almost as the characters do.
[It's] about characters who insist on trying to exert their freewill despite living in a world in which they have none - that itself is never insistent.
It's gorgeous to look at and, even though the plot might seem flimsy, it speaks with authority and says much about big business and the times lived, not just back then but now.

Every moment of exposition, every flare-up of personality: none of it comes off as mere talk, no bit of swindling feels as straightforward as a mere "Gotcha!" plot twist. It always feels active, alert, contained, stylish.
This movie intentionally doesn't offer the pure dopamine hit of Ocean's Eleven, but Soderbergh's ability to play so broadly within a single genre is just as thrilling.
The film's got plenty of ideas that you've heard before. (All it needs is Mark Ruffalo popping in to scream, "The system is rigged!")
With One Sudden Move, Steven Soderbergh mixes an old-school 1950s noir with a modern sense of social self-consciousness.

"No Sudden Move" offers a look at a city in a period of transition and what that transition does to everyone around it. The big beats crackle, the smaller ones hang around like an aftershock. Don't be surprised if it ends up knocking you out.

title: The Ice Road | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The ratio of exposition-heavy dialogue to things-a-real-person-would-say lines is roughly 20 to 1. Any bit of visual wit that manages to slip through feels accidental.
The setup has potential, with trapped miners needing saving but icy roads making rescue efforts difficult. But it hits the skids and ends up formulaic and cliched.
Piles cliches atop cliches with an end result of mush - not content to be the story of a dramatic rescue, it's also a conspiracy movie and a revenge thriller.
The film arguably works best prior to this gearshift, when it appears to be primarily about keeping huge vehicles moving steadily and horizontally rather than abruptly and vertically.
The Ice Road doesn't share a trucker's discipline, and it speeds up and up and up until it bleeds into a different, more conventional action sub-genre altogether.
This is a big, dumb, often gripping action movie.

Neeson's durability as an action hero seems more remarkable as the years go on. Yes, he's older and brittler and paler here... But, just like Mike, he gets the job done, and he's the reason to watch this.
[It] has its blunt charms, and offers more than one instance of Neeson punching a guy in the face. And admit it: that's part of what you came here for, isn't it?

[Neeson's] action hero schtick... has become so repetitive that one imagines him just shuffling from one set to the other dragging his rifle, wearing the same costume, each role boringly interchangeable.
As The Ice Road goes on, [its] matter-of-fact approach increasingly feels at odds with what's happening onscreen. Such a smart movie probably shouldn't have been so stupid.

Simply put, Neeson has been in a bit of a rut, one that Ice Road exemplifies almost literally, since at several points in the movie the challenge involves extricating big trucks from slushy situations.
But while the Irish actor reliably hits both his marks and the bad guys, he's doing so in a film that's leadenly predictable when it's not unintentionally laugh-out-loud funny.
The by-the-numbers screenplay feels predictable from first moment to last.
The film lacks slam-bang, signature action sequences that would make it more memorable.
"The Ice Road" is what we used to call a B-movie, but there's no shame in a B-movie that carries out its mission with such competence and star power.
An increasingly implausible action movie that will entertain most viewers, but also perhaps make them feel a bit played for fools.
Even "The Ice Road's" dumbest turns are stabilized by the presence of Neeson, a real Kenworth of a man if there ever was one. Even when big rigs are dieseling next to him, he commands the screen.
Despite its many perils, both natural and human, The Ice Road is surprisingly dull. It's definitely not as crazy as it should have been, given the setting and the stakes.
Sadly, Neeson's dander is no match for a hackneyed plot, poorly visualized stunts and characters whose behavior can defy common sense.
The film is a muddle of clichés and unremarkable action sequences that bleed together into a cacophony.

title: I Carry You With Me | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A fascinating - though at times uneven - blend of film styles.
This flawed but powerful immigrant love story is worthy of the big screen.
The overall feeling here is ethereal, dreamy, moody, memory-like -- a more user-friendly Terence Malick vibe. It is a gorgeous film, and one that deserves to be seen on a giant screen.
Admirable efforts aside, I Carry You With Me is still an enchanting mix of drama and romance, but also a timely, poetic love letter to Iván's home country, Mexico
The film is a big hug, but the "you" of the title is a homeland, and it is many miles away.
If you're a sucker for love stories about couples overcoming obstacles, Heidi Ewing's low-key indie is a find.
Dreams make up both the form and substance of "I Carry You With Me," Heidi Ewing's accomplished narrative feature debut.
Most of the time, the effect is exhilarating: a surreal concoction that packs a considerable punch in the film's final moments.
With its ability to evoke common feelings while dramatizing a unique point of view, film is an excellent vehicle for empathy-especially when a filmmaker makes that their guiding artistic principle...
Director Heidi Ewing makes a powerful narrative debut with I Carry You with Me, a dreamy and tender, decades-spanning story about love, sacrifice, memory and immigration.
It's so lovely. It's a very intimate and empathetic depiction of this love story that is true.

The documentary and narrative pieces of I Carry You with Me don't always fit neatly together, but the performances, hand-held camerawork, simple truths of prejudice, poverty, and peril make it easy to glide past rough patches.
I Carry You With Me is a complicated film, in many ways, and it covers a lot of ground, but the emotions portrayed are simple and human-sized.
Its imperfections and its beauties are inextricable from each other, and also from the sad, inspiring real-life story it has to tell.
[I Carry You with Me] is so heartfelt, and the material so intrinsically powerful, that I Carry You With Me slowly catches up with itself, and lights a fire fueled by food and love.

Turning time and memory into an elliptical portrait of what it means when borders become barriers, "I Carry You With Me," the first narrative feature from the documentary filmmaker Heidi Ewing, trades distance for empathy.
We've all heard the horror stories, but these small cruelties become just as heartbreaking - especially when rendered so viscerally and elegantly on film.
It's innovative, amazing and hybrid filmmaking by first-time director Heidi Ewing.
Heidi Ewing's tale of immigration and deportation afflicting the lives of a Mexican gay couple flashes its reason for being at every turn.

The love story of Ivan and Gerardo is an important one, and by sharing it, Ewing brings attention to the challenges facing LGBTQ people in Mexico, encouraging empathy for those who feel compelled to flee to the U.S. in order to live openly.

title: Salvador | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Of Stone's two recent films, Salvador is the most remarkable, if only for its drive and sense of attack, its willingness to deal in current politics as directly as it does.
Although it doesn't attain the stature of The Killing Fields, the film is an effective comment on the actions in Central America.
The polemic may seem obvious and at times laboured, but the action sequences are brilliant, and the film does achieve a brutal, often very moving, power.
The tale of American photojournalist Richard Boyle's adventures in strife-torn Central America, Salvador is as raw, difficult, compelling, unreasonable, reckless and vivid as its protagonist.
One look at the youthful, idealistic guerrillas, accompanied everywhere by folk music, and you know where Mr. Stone's heart lies.
Salvador is long and disjointed and tries to tell too many stories... But the heart of the movie is fascinating.

title: Werewolves Within | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's a film that wants to please and to some extent succeeds in doing so, without ever being very funny or very alarming.
Starring a delightful Sam Richardson, at its best Werewolves Within feels like a cross between the 1987 vampire film The Lost Boys and the 2002 and 2004 live-action Scooby-Doo films.
This goofy horror comedy, based on an online game of the same name, just goes to prove that if you have a great cast, smart direction and witty script you can just about get away with murder.
Werewolves Within is fun without ever rising to frightening or frightfully funny.
A new comedy classic whodunnit in the honored tradition of Clue, Werewolves Within finds the laughs in the jump scare, and brings back the uproarious joy of the "it's behind you!" creeping fright.
She's equal parts angel and devil, and as the counterpoint to Richardson's plucky go-get-'em do-gooder, Vayntrub is a bedeviling ingénue who's the ideal yin to his yang.
A goofy and skillful [horror story], with a lot of charisma across the board to paper over its shortcomings.
Both funny and snappy, the horror-comedy "Werewolves Within" isn't just easy to like, it's easy to "get."
"Werewolves Within" joins the rarified club of video game film adaptations that don't make me want to gouge my eyes out.
The film possesses a strong touch of Edgar Wright in how it manages both the humor and horror of its conceit...
The film becomes unexpectedly, effectively violent just when you've written it off as a glorified SNL sketch.
This overstuffed script drips with blink-and-you'll-miss-them jokes that lampoon everything and challenge nothing, least of all monstrosity itself.
With a dream cast and a shrewd commentary on our fractious times, "Werewolves Within" is delightful, one the best surprises of 2021.
The sole purpose of this hysterical horror comedy is to perfectly deliver the right amount of gore and guffaws.

Sam Richardson shows off his delightfully understated demeanor as the lone voice of reason in this town of oddballs and malcontents, proving to be the most entertaining element of a strained whodunit.
That starts with Richardson, who steps into a leading role with more than enough charisma and clear-eyed goodness to anchor the rest of Ruben's ensemble cast.
Unafraid to sink its teeth into current affairs, "Werewolves Within"... has the kind of sharp bite that feels fresh, even fearless.
Ruben's latest plays like a joyous hug of a comedy-horror movie full of charisma, violent antics, and entertaining character-driven mystery.

title: Mary J. Blige's My Life | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This new documentary is utterly riveting as Blige recalls a childhood marked by violence and abuse in a grim New York housing project, and how she emerged with deep psychological issues unprepared for the success of her debut album.
With "My Life," Blige saved herself -- and reminded her fans their selves were worth saving as well
We never really get a sense of where she's been, let alone My Life's musical and cultural context.
The sheen of a highly controlled narrative glosses over this 82-minute documentary.
Where the documentary succeeds most plangently is in its fan testimonials of the album's impact and Blige's emotional recollections of the songs' roots.

title: America: The Motion Picture | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Most of the time, it's knowingly stupid, which makes watching it 90 minutes of occasional fun and frequent indifference.
Even when you think it's only acting rude and juvenile just because, it's much smarter than that, particularly whenever it skewers American attitudes (both conservative and liberal).

Rarely have I seen a movie so confident that its audience not only revels in American benightedness but is eager to identify with it. That makes America: The Motion Picture not only a waste of time but an insult to ignoramuses.
Though loyalists and sticklers for historical accuracy may not consider it their cup of tea, "America" will likely win over anyone who knows not to take it too seriously.
Just a mess.

A rowdy sendup of the country's id. Eagles scream. "Free Bird" wails. Paul Bunyan boxes Big Ben. And in a nod to America's ill-informed history classes, Washington also stutters his goal to do "something about taxation?"
Everyone here seems to really get what [director Matt Thompson] is going for, embracing the dumb side of America while playing some of its most historic figures.
The movie tries to outrace its own jokes before they run into a ditch. It's not easy: The element of surprise -- the foul-mouthed Founding Fathers, for instance -- lasts only so long.
The gulf between stupid-smart and just plain stupid feels immeasurably vast when watching "America: The Motion Picture," which is clearly aiming for the former but lands squarely in the latter.
Thompson and Miller/Lord make for a natural pairing, though the same can't be said of screenwriter Dave Callaham, the clear wrench in the machinery.
